tldr: This paper presents DexFormer 2.0, a method that controls 24 combinations of 4 robot arms and 6 dexterous hands with a single reinforcement learning policy, adapting to unseen arm-hand pairings and completely new hands without any fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DexFormer 2.0. Input arm and hand joints are mapped onto a shared interface with up to 29 degrees of freedom. Passing through the kinematic-tree-aware spatial encoder MorphNode and a Transformer-XL holding short-term memory, a single shared actor directly outputs target joint angles for all joints.
overview:
Dexterous grasping with multi-fingered hands is one of the most challenging tasks in robotics. Conventionally, reinforcement learning policies have been trained specifically for a fixed pair of one arm and one hand. Whenever an arm or hand is replaced with a different model, the degrees of freedom, joint arrangements, limits, and contact dynamics change fundamentally. This forced researchers to retrain models from scratch for every new piece of hardware.

To solve this, the authors developed DexFormer 2.0, which drives diverse combinations of arms and hands using a single shared policy and generalizes zero-shot to unseen hardware combinations. The key idea is standardizing all robots into a canonical joint interface of up to 29 slots (7 arm axes + up to 22 hand axes) with validity masks. It embeds joint-level physical descriptors (rotation axis, range of motion, kinematic tree depth, etc.) and integrates tree-structural distances directly into the attention mechanism. Furthermore, a Transformer-XL maintains short-term interaction history to infer embodiment-dependent dynamic responses during contact in real time, going beyond static morphological descriptions.

In simulation, the policy was trained on 18 out of 24 possible combinations (4 arms and 6 hands). Evaluated on the remaining 6 held-out pairs, it achieved a 51.18% grasping success rate. It also succeeded in grasping with 4 completely unseen hand types without fine-tuning, retargeting motions to two-jaw parallel grippers, and transferring zero-shot to physical hardware, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of a cross-embodiment dexterous grasping policy.
contributions: Established a unified cross-embodiment learning paradigm that trains a single reinforcement learning policy across diverse morphologies (4 arms and 6 dexterous hands) and transfers to unseen combinations and novel hands.

Proposed an embodiment-aware recurrent architecture combining joint-level physical descriptors, spatial attention biased by kinematic tree distances, and Transformer-XL to infer dynamic contact responses from past interactions.
Demonstrated through ablation studies that temporal memory, the kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each play a critical role in cross-embodiment generalization.

Distilled the simulation-trained privileged policy into a depth-based student model, validating zero-shot transfer on a physical Flexiv arm with two different hands, including a held-out pairing, without any real-world training.

sections.heading: Ending the era of retraining policies from scratch for every robot
sections.summary: Dexterous grasping has traditionally relied heavily on specific hardware setups, requiring a brand new policy whenever an arm or hand is swapped. This paper presents DexFormer 2.0, a single shared policy that controls diverse arm-hand combinations and generalizes zero-shot to unseen pairings and novel hands.
sections.details:
Dexterous grasping policies with robotic hands have historically been developed for fixed hardware pairs consisting of one specific arm and one specific hand. However, retraining a policy every time a new arm or hand enters a lab or factory leads to a combinatorial explosion in training cost. It also prevents roboticists from sharing motion skill knowledge across different hardware platforms.

Controlling different arm-hand systems with a single policy is notoriously difficult for three main reasons. First, because active joint counts and layouts vary across hands, observation and action spaces share no common interface. Second, even with identical control signals, differences in rotation axes, ranges of motion, link lengths, and hierarchy depths mean completely different physical motions. Third, geometric information alone is insufficient; dynamic behaviors such as reaction forces and friction during contact must be inferred in real time from recent interaction history.

DexFormer 2.0 tackles these three hurdles cleanly. It represents all robots through 29 canonical slots (7 for the arm and 22 for the hand) with validity masks, annotating each joint with physical descriptors like axis orientation, position, limits, and depth. By combining MorphNode, which performs spatial attention based on kinematic tree connectivity, with Transformer-XL, which maintains the past 16 steps of history, a single actor network successfully controls diverse robot morphologies.

sections.heading: From single-robot mastery to cross-embodiment generalist control
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning for dexterous manipulation has made great strides, most works have focused solely on generalizing to novel objects on a single robot. This study extends the cross-embodiment paradigm, previously explored in quadruped locomotion, to the much harder domain of coordinated arm and multi-fingered hand control.
sections.details:
### Dexterous grasping and sim-to-real transfer
Combining reinforcement learning with domain randomization has enabled sophisticated real-world manipulation with robotic hands. Frameworks such as UniDexGrasp and UniDexGrasp++ have improved generalization across diverse object geometries. However, they were all built on top of a single fixed robot setup. In other words, while generalizing across objects has been widely studied, generalizing across robot hardware remained largely unaddressed.

### Generalist policies across embodiments
Hardware-agnostic control policies have primarily progressed in mobile robotics, such as quadrupedal locomotion. Message-passing graph neural networks over joints and Transformer architectures treating joints as tokens have been proposed. Recent large-scale imitation learning models have also targeted generalist manipulation, but most focus on simple two-jaw parallel grippers and cannot handle the intricate contact control demanded by multi-fingered hands.

### Cross-embodiment dexterous control
Prior attempts at cross-hand control include CrossDex, which retargets hand motions via human hand synergies, as well as GET-Zero and DexGrasp-Zero, which utilize hand kinematic graphs. However, these methods rely on Cartesian wrist poses or fix the arm in place. DexFormer 2.0 goes far beyond them: it achieves direct joint-space control across 24 full-body arm-hand combinations spanning 4 arms (Flexiv, Franka, KUKA, xArm7) and 6 hands (Revo3, Sharpa, LEAP, Allegro, RAPID, Shadow) using one unified policy.

sections.heading: How DexFormer 2.0 works: canonical slots, tree bias, and temporal memory
sections.summary: Robot joints are mapped onto a 29-slot canonical interface and tagged with physical descriptors. Using the topology-aware MorphNode spatial encoder and a 16-step Transformer-XL memory, a single shared actor generates target joint angles across various embodiments.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
An embodiment $e=(a,h)$ is defined by pairing an arm $a$ with a hand $h$. The goal is to obtain a single stochastic policy $\pi_{\theta}$ that directly controls any embodiment $e$. All robots are mapped to a canonical 29-joint interface containing 7 arm slots and 22 hand slots. A binary mask $\mathbf{v}_e$ is applied to unused slots, zeroing out their observations, features, and actions so that absent joints never disrupt learning.

### 3.2 Joint-Level Morphology Representation
Each joint $i$ receives a 16-dimensional morphology descriptor $\mathbf{m}_i$. This descriptor includes the rotation axis in the parent link frame (3D), anchor position (3D), joint limit center and span (2D), velocity limit (1D), a one-hot identity vector indicating arm or finger role (6D), and depth in the kinematic tree (1D). Providing local physical parameters rather than arbitrary robot IDs allows knowledge to transfer to unseen robots. Concatenating these descriptors with the joint's current angle, velocity, previous action, and end-effector position (6D) yields a 22-dimensional feature vector per joint.

### 3.3 MorphNode Spatial Encoder
The spatial encoder MorphNode consists of two branches: an MLP body encoder and a topology-aware MorphAttention residual block. MorphAttention computes self-attention across 34 tokens, consisting of the 29 joint tokens plus 5 task tokens (object state, goal pose, contact forces, etc.). A soft bias based on the topological graph distance in the kinematic tree and role relations (same finger, different fingers, arm-hand) is added to the attention matrix. This naturally encourages coordination among physically connected joints.

### 3.4 & 3.5 Temporal Context and Actor Head
Spatial features are fed into a 3-layer, 8-head Transformer-XL. By retaining a Key/Value memory cache over the last 16 steps, it implicitly infers contact dynamics and response delays that cannot be captured by static kinematic descriptions alone. Finally, these features are concatenated with processed task observations, and a shared actor head outputs actions (relative joint target angles) for all 29 degrees of freedom at once.

### 3.6 Training Objective
The policy is trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). During each rollout, diverse arm-hand combinations are mixed and simulated concurrently. This funnels policy gradients from all embodiments into a single network, enabling robust cross-embodiment reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Impressive generalization: unseen pairs, novel hands, and zero-shot sim-to-real
sections.summary: Trained on 18 out of 24 pairings and evaluated on the remaining 6 held-out pairs, the method substantially outperformed baselines. It also succeeded in zero-shot transfer to 4 unseen hands and a physical robot setup (Flexiv arm + Revo3/LEAP hands).
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted in Isaac Lab across 24 combinations pairing 4 arms (Flexiv, Franka, KUKA, xArm7) with 6 hands (Revo3, Sharpa, LEAP, Allegro, RAPID, Shadow). 18 combinations were used for training and 6 were held out for testing. Performance was evaluated using the Stable Success Rate (SR), defined as completing a 240-step trajectory while keeping object position error within 5 cm over the final 30 steps.

### 4.2 Comparison with Baselines
The proposed method (Ours) was compared against an MLP + GRU baseline and DexFormer 1.0 (which lacks morphology descriptors). On seen objects, it reached an 89.01% success rate on seen pairings and 51.18% on held-out pairings (compared to 31.28% for GRU and 14.15% for DexFormer 1.0). Under the most challenging condition—unseen YCB objects on held-out pairings—it maintained a 48.85% success rate, outperforming GRU (33.18%) by 15.67 percentage points.

### 4.3 Ablation Study
Ablation experiments confirmed the necessity of each architectural component. Disabling the Transformer-XL memory reduced held-out pairing SR by 26.73 percentage points, and removing the kinematic-tree bias dropped performance by 27.03 percentage points. Removing the MorphAttention residual block entirely (MLP + TXL) crashed SR down to 18.90%, proving that both topology-aware spatial attention and temporal memory are essential for generalization.

### 4.4 & 4.5 Coverage and Unseen Hands
Increasing the number of training pairings from 6 to 12 and 18 caused held-out success rates to surge from 0.07% to 5.65% and then to 51.18%. Because all individual arms and hands were present from the start, this highlights that combination coverage is the true key to generalization. In zero-shot evaluation on 4 completely unseen hands (Wuji 1, Tesollo, XHAND1, Revo2), the policy reached an average success rate of 17.45% (peaking at 27.18% on Wuji 1). Furthermore, retargeting through a virtual LEAP hand enabled opening and closing control of two-jaw parallel grippers.

### 4.6 & 4.7 Faults and Real-World Experiments
The policy also showed high robustness in joint-freezing fault-tolerance tests. For real-world experiments, the privileged simulation policy was distilled via DAgger into a depth-conditioned student model and deployed on a physical Flexiv arm with Revo3 and LEAP hands. Without any real-world fine-tuning, it achieved high grasping and basket-transport success rates: 92% (23/25 trials) on the seen LEAP pairing and 68% (17/25 trials) on the held-out Revo3 pairing.

captions.F5: Training curves showing grasp success rate and mean episode reward across 18 training combinations. DexFormer 2.0 (blue solid line) learns substantially faster and achieves higher performance than the tree-bias-free ablation (red dashed line), GRU, and DexFormer 1.0 baselines.
captions.F7: Real-world grasping and basket-transport task on a tabletop setup with a physical Flexiv arm. Top: held-out Revo3 hand. Bottom: seen LEAP hand. Both setups stably lift diverse real-world objects.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A solid stride toward generalist dexterous manipulation
sections.summary: DexFormer 2.0 achieves cross-embodiment control over diverse arm-hand systems by combining a canonical interface, joint-level physical descriptors, topology-aware attention, and temporal memory. Strong generalization to unseen pairings and hands, along with zero-shot real-world transfer, provides a powerful stepping stone toward future foundation policies in robotics.
sections.details:
The core insight demonstrated by this work is that when supplied with a canonical interface and the right physical and topological inductive biases, a single neural network can naturally accommodate the kinematic diversity of disparate robot embodiments.

Achieving over 51% grasp success on held-out pairs, along with successful transfer to unseen hands, grippers, and real-world hardware through joint training of 4 arms and 6 hands, provides strong momentum for robot foundation policies. Moving away from the inefficient cycle of retraining bespoke policies for every hardware change, this work marks an important milestone toward a future where a single model operates across any robotic body.

takeaways: Combining a canonical slot interface with joint-level physical descriptors (axis, limits, tree depth) enables a single network to unify multi-fingered robots across different kinematic layouts.
Injecting topological kinematic tree distance into attention biases and equipping the model with Transformer-XL memory to infer contact dynamics are essential for robust cross-embodiment transfer.
Cross-embodiment generalization depends heavily on the coverage of arm-hand pairings during training, with performance on unseen pairs improving dramatically as pairing combinations increase.

Privileged cross-embodiment policies trained in simulation can be distilled into depth-based student models that transfer zero-shot to physical robots with high reliability without real-world fine-tuning.
limitations: The grasp success rate on unseen arm-hand pairings is around 51%, leaving an approximate 38-percentage-point performance gap compared to seen pairings (~89%).

Zero-shot grasp success on completely novel hands averages 17.45%, suggesting that practical deployment on unseen hands will still require light fine-tuning or broader morphological diversity during training.

Support for parallel grippers relies on motion retargeting through a virtual LEAP hand rather than direct control, meaning it does not represent true cross-embodiment policy execution for two-jaw grippers.
